chapter: Brass bands, Eddie Miller and band stories
title: Billy Braun and the Spinsters Ball in Biloxi
summary: Story of a carnival ball in Biloxi where a novelty band upstaged Brownlee's seasoned band until Ray Baduc's dance saved the night; his advice to do something besides play.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Didn't you have a malaphone player one time?
Oh, yes, and a very, one of the finest. He played, he played saxophone parts. And many times, he'd switch over. Uh, here's a switch for you. Uh, he'd play piano. Billy Braun.
Oh, that's who I was trying to think.

Billy Braun, he played piano. And, uh, many times, rehearse the band with, uh, numbers. A new number come out, Billy would play it, see? And we might say, play it again. And he'd play it again, and, uh, then, uh, then we'd take it. He'd switch over. But, uh, we were playing, uh, we were playing the, uh, the Spinsters Ball in, uh, Biloxi, Mississippi. A carnival ball. And they had two bands. They had my band, and I had a, I had a very good aggregation there that night from the sense of musicians. I mean, it was like, like Pinky Vedakovich on sax and Jordy on sax. And, uh, uh, Baduk on drums, Billy Braun on mellophone, uh, Joe Lorcanna trombone. And, uh, I don't know whether, whether Chink was playing bass with us that night or not. I believe he was. I believe Chink was playing bass. Joe Capriero was playing guitar. And, uh, we were really riding out, and it was really fun. And I was playing piano. Well, uh, they had another little band over there that had just organized. Johnny Tobin.

And Mike Holloway. And they all had brand new instruments. Uh, very fine instruments, too. Very polished and all that. And they had little funny hats to put on, and, and they did things, you know. They put on funny hats, and then they'd, uh, uh, one boy played, uh, accordion. He swapped over and played accordion, uh, loud and wrong, but he played accordion, squeeze box, you know. And, uh, people were eating that up. And here we were with a seasoned band. And, uh, I had always advocated you had to do a little something different than just playing music. I don't care whether it's putting on the funny hat or the funny nose or the, uh, a couple of little, little steps around and just do a little something, uh, aside from actually playing your music to more or less entertain a little bit, to take the monotony away of just that straight rhythm all the way. Mm-hmm . He got out and he got a little audience in front of the bandstand. He did a little dance out there, a little slew foot dance. I got over on drums and Billy Braun got on the piano. And Ray was out there dancing. Well, they applauded him and they gave him a little bit more room. And he did some more antics. He was funny. He could really maneuver his body. It was recognized as something different. So then finally everybody cleared back, all the way back, and gave him the whole ballroom. And he danced from one corner of that ballroom to the other and back and then finally wound up like as though he pulled a comb out of his pocket as though he was playing flute and went down behind the drums.
Just fell out on the floor right now.

He was tired anyhow. Well, that saved the day. They all went wild as to what we could do. And then Loyal Canna, of course, he played a little trombone with his, took his shoes off and played slide with his feet, which was nothing. But I mean he could do it very easily. But they ate it up. And so they kept us the hour and let the other boys go home. But that was the only reason the way we saved face was by doing a little stunt other than just playing music. Now, we definitely had the best orchestra. Those boys were just starting in the business. I guess it was one of their first jobs. And, of course, they were all fine boys, don't get me wrong. But that's how things can happen. And my suggestion to any orchestra, do something. I don't care if it's just make a handstand, but do something other than just play your instrument. I've advocated it since I can remember myself. I always said that you had to do something different. So, we saved face that night.
